# Ellipsoidal profile reduction and an exact obstruction to one pre-stationary multiplier

This note concerns the ordinary weighted stationary-section problem. It does not assert a mixed-integer depth theorem. Its positive result invokes the already proved rank-two theorem in `candidate 3ed6256a0896f434`, §5. Its negative result is an exact uniform planar example; no numerical calculation enters its proof.

## 1. Ellipsoidal homothetic profiles reduce to rank two

Let d=m+1>=2. Let D be a centered ellipsoid in R^m, let r be positive and concave on [a,b], where a<0<b, and put

    K={(X,z):a<=z<=b, X in r(z)D}.

For each member of a finite menu, let u_i be a unit inward normal, let S_i be the (d-1)-volume of K intersect u_i^perp, and let p_i be the fraction of K captured by u_i.X>=0. Assume each section has centroid zero. If theta_i>=0, sum theta_i=1, and

    sum_i theta_i S_i u_i=0,

then

    sum_i theta_i p_i >= gamma_d.

Here gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d. In fact the archived argument gives 4/9 when d=2, 3/7 when 3<=d<=9, and 2/5 when d>=10. The argument does not give a dimension-free 4/9.

Proof. First apply a fixed invertible linear transformation of the horizontal coordinates taking D to a Euclidean ball. This is an ordinary continuous theorem, so no lattice is involved. To track the balance exactly, if the full transformation is T, a raw old normal N becomes N'=T^{-T}N. Raw coarea transforms as

    (S'/|N'|)=|det T|(S/|N|).

Consequently its section-gradient vector becomes |det T| T^{-T} times the old vector. The given balance, section centroids, and cap fractions are preserved.

In the ball coordinates write each unit normal as (c_i,b_i), with c_i in R^m. Horizontally rotate its cap and section so c_i becomes |c_i|e_1. Rotational invariance of K preserves S_i, p_i, and the zero section centroid. Replace this rotated cap by its two horizontal reflections with weights theta_i/2. Their horizontal gradient vectors cancel. Their combined vertical gradient is the original theta_i S_i b_i. The original balance therefore proves that the entire replacement menu balances. All replacement normals lie in span{e_1,e_z}, and every replacement section is still centered at zero. The archived rank-two theorem now applies and proves the assertions. Caps with c_i=0 simply produce two identical copies, and caps with b_i=0 pose no exception. QED.

## 2. The exact interval-layer normalization

For a general centrally symmetric D, fix a horizontal direction. Its one-dimensional projection density is even and unimodal; after normalization it is a mixture of uniform laws on centered intervals [-R,R]. A layer of radius R, under x=R X, gives the SAME planar density

    f(X,z)=(1/2) r(z)^(m-1) 1_{|X|<=r(z)}.

Every layer has total mass V=int_a^b r(z)^m dz. Only the slope of a cap changes: z+t x>=0 becomes z+s X>=0, with s=tR.

Define the unnormalized cap mass P(s), raw section coarea C(s), and vertical section first moment M(s) for this common density by

    P(s)=int 1_{z+sX>=0} f(X,z)dX dz,
    C(s)=int delta(z+sX) f(X,z)dX dz,
    M(s)=int z delta(z+sX) f(X,z)dX dz.

The delta notation is precisely integration over the line divided by the raw normal length sqrt(1+s^2). It can equivalently be defined by the ordinary coarea formula. The relation z=-sX on the section implies

    M(s)=-s int X delta(z+sX) f(X,z)dX dz.

Thus actual centering of a mixed interval-layer section forces the average of M(s) to vanish. It does NOT force the section of each interval component to be centered.

A sufficient, stronger auxiliary statement would be existence of two real numbers c,lambda, depending on the common profile, such that for every s>=0,

    (4/9)V <= P(s)-c C(s)-lambda M(s) <= (5/9)V.       (1)

The coarea correction would cancel under reflected normal balance, and the first-moment correction would cancel under centering. The next exact example shows that (1) is false even for m=1.

## 3. An exact concave planar profile

Take r to be the piecewise affine function through

    (-8,15), (-2,20), (-1,15), (1,3).

Its slopes are 5/6,-5,-6, so r is positive and concave. Let K={(x,z):|x|<=r(z), -8<=z<=1}, with density 1/2. Its total mass is

    V=int r(z)dz=105+35/2+18=281/2.

For the three positive-z caps at slopes 0, 1/10, and 3/5, the exact data are

| s | P(s) | C(s) | M(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 6 | 9 | 0 |
| 1/10 | 607/64 | 205/16 | -4715/512 |
| 3/5 | 44 | 15/2 | -105/4 |

Here is a direct verification. At s=0, r(0)=9 and int_0^1 r=6. For s>0 the line exists precisely at those z with |z|<=s r(z); on that interval its raw coarea density is 1/(2s), and its vertical first-moment density is z/(2s). At s=1/10 the interval is [-2,9/16], giving the displayed C and M. The cap is empty below -2, is partially captured with width-density (r(z)+10z)/2 up to 9/16, and fully captured above 9/16. Integrating on the affine pieces gives 607/64. At s=3/5 the entire axial interval [-8,1] is partially captured: endpoint inequalities hold, and concavity ensures |z|<s r(z) between them. Thus

    P=(1/2) int_{-8}^1 [r(z)+(5/3)z]dz=44,
    C=9/(2(3/5))=15/2,
    M=(1/(2(3/5))) int_{-8}^1 z dz=-105/4.

## 4. Contradiction to the common two-multiplier bound

Put mu_s=M(s)/C(s). Dividing (1) by C(s)>0 shows that c+lambda mu_s must lie in the interval

    [(P(s)-(5/9)V)/C(s), (P(s)-(4/9)V)/C(s)].

The relevant exact entries are

| s | mu_s | lower endpoint | upper endpoint |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | -1297/162 | -508/81 |
| 1/10 | -23/32 | -39497/7380 | -6101/1476 |
| 3/5 | -7/2 | -613/135 | -332/135 |

The lower bound at 1/10 and upper bound at 3/5 imply

    lambda >= -512344/492615.

The lower bound at 1/10 and upper bound at 0 imply

    lambda <= -488696/381915.

But the first bound minus the second equals

    8142208/33990435 > 0.

No pair (c,lambda) satisfies (1).

Equivalently, the separating finite menu is explicit. Give total weight 16128/40031 to the REVERSED slope-1/10 pair, total weight 5658/40031 to the positive slope-3/5 pair, and weight 18245/40031 to the positive horizontal cap. Split each nonhorizontal weight equally between its two horizontal reflections. Then both the signed raw vertical coarea and the signed vertical section first moment sum to zero. The horizontal gradient balance holds by reflection. Yet the captured mean is

    4942884/11248711
       =4/9-508888/101238399 <4/9.

The individual slope-1/10 and slope-3/5 sections are NOT centered. This is therefore not a counterexample to the stationary-section theorem or to the original homothetic-profile target. It precisely blocks replacing individual section centering by one aggregate first-moment constraint in the proposed universal component inequality.

## 5. Scope of the remaining problem

The positive ellipsoid theorem uses genuine symmetry to transport each centered section to one common plane. General interval-layer decompositions do not preserve that property component by component. The exact counterexample shows that adding one universal linear multiplier for their vertical first moments does not repair this loss at the dimension-free constant 4/9. Section 6 below separately tests the correct tied exponent and ambient constant. A mechanism using the actual direction-dependent layer distributions, additional constraints on those distributions, or a different non-linear moment penalty is not excluded here.

## 6. The correct density exponent and Gamma_3 also have an exact obstruction

The preceding m=1 example must not be used to infer failure for the relevant m>=2 density r^(m-1) and smaller ambient constant gamma_(m+1). That correctly paired statement nevertheless has a different, simpler exact counterexample.

Take m=2, d=3, r(z)=1-z on [-3,1/2], and

    f(x,z)=(1-z)/2 on |x|<=1-z, -3<=z<=1/2.

The profile is affine and strictly positive on the entire closed interval. This is precisely the common interval-layer density required in dimension three, with total mass

    V=int_{-3}^{1/2}(1-z)^2 dz=511/24.

For 0<=s<=3/4, the section z+s x=0 ranges from -s/(1-s) to s/(1+s). Neither endpoint is removed by the axial truncation. Integrating the section density (1-z)/(2s), continuously interpreted at s=0, gives

    C(s)=1/(1-s^2)^2,
    M(s)=-4s^2/[3(1-s^2)^3].

In the full triangle extending to z=1 the corresponding cap mass is C(s)/3, as follows either by direct integration or by the elementary cone formula. The removed top triangle contributes int_(1/2)^1 (1-z)^2 dz=1/24 and is fully captured by all these caps. Consequently

    P(s)=C(s)/3-1/24.

In particular the complete exact data are

| s | P(s) | C(s) | M(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7/24 | 1 | 0 |
| 1/2 | 119/216 | 16/9 | -64/81 |
| 3/4 | 1999/1176 | 256/49 | -3072/343 |

Suppose there were c,lambda such that for every s>=0,

    (27/64)V <= P(s)-c C(s)-lambda M(s) <= (37/64)V.   (2)

Apply the lower inequality to the positive caps of slopes 0 and 3/4, and the equivalent lower inequality to the REVERSED cap of slope 1/2. Give those three types integer weights 5120,343,3888 respectively. The signed coarea and moment corrections cancel exactly:

    5120*1 +343*(256/49) -3888*(16/9)
      =5120+1792-6912=0,

    343*(-3072/343) -3888*(-64/81)
      =-3072+3072=0.

Dividing by the total weight 9351 and by V, (2) would therefore imply that the resulting captured mean is at least 27/64. But direct substitution gives

    [5120*(7/24)+343*(1999/1176)
          +3888*(511/24-119/216)]/[(9351)(511/24)]
      =31511/75847
      =27/64-31165/4854208 <27/64.                  (3)

This contradicts (2). Splitting both oblique weights equally between horizontally reflected caps gives full normal balance; the raw vertical section moments still cancel with the displayed signs.

Thus even the correct dimension-three exponent and exact gamma_3 cannot be established by this universal two-multiplier component inequality. The counterexample is a truncated affine profile, not merely a nonaffine one. As before, the individual oblique sections have nonzero first moment. Equation (3) does not contradict the stationary-section theorem for pyramids or prove failure for any actual individually centered layer mixture.
